notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 11, drawn from the permitted sources:

---

## Structure and Context

Before the verse-by-verse notes, several commentators point out a structural issue. **Verses 1–3 are widely understood as parenthetical**: they record a revelation God gave Moses *before* his final confrontation with Pharaoh, inserted here to explain Moses' confidence. The actual speech to Pharaoh resumes in v.4 from the confrontation of Exodus 10:24–29. **J. Ligon Duncan** (cited at Precept Austin) explains: "If you look at Exodus 11:1-3, they basically serve as a parenthesis... Then in Exodus 11:4-8, the plague is actually announced in the presence of Pharaoh. All of this is happening before Moses leaves." So does the **Believer's Study Bible**, **Ellicott**, and **Whedon**. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html

**Verses 9–10** are a summary of all nine previous plagues and their effect on Pharaoh, closing the narrative before the Passover account begins. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html

---

## v. 1: "I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt one more plague… he will drive you out completely."

- **God's guarantee of success.** Precept Austin notes that God had already revealed this to Moses at the burning bush (Ex 3:20), so "from the get-go God promises Moses, you will be successful, you will win this battle." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **"Drive you out completely"** (Hebrew: "in thrusting he shall thrust you out"). Gill says this means the expulsion would be absolute, unlimited, unconditional—no restrictions on children, flocks, or any condition of return. Pharaoh would expel them with "force and vehemence, with urgency and in great haste." Currid (cited at Precept Austin) notes Pharaoh had previously tried partial concessions (no children, no flocks, not far away), but now "the Israelites will leave Egypt in totality." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-11.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **The Hebrew word for "plague"** here is *nega* (not the usual *maggephah*), related to "touch." It is the only use of *nega* in Exodus and first appears in Genesis 12:17 when God struck Pharaoh's house for Sarai's sake. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary

---

## v. 2: "Ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold."

- **Not "borrowing."** The KJV's "borrow" is misleading; the Hebrew *sha'al* means "ask" or "demand." Ellicott, Whedon, and the NET Notes agree: this was a request for gifts from terror-stricken Egyptians who knew Israel was leaving forever. There was no expectation of return. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **Fair compensation, not theft.** David Guzik (Enduring Word): "The plundering of Egypt wasn't theft but fair compensation—Israel received wages for their labor as slaves, and these treasures later adorned the Sanctuary and the High Priest's breastplate." Henry Morris and W.A. Criswell agree: this was just payment for centuries of unpaid forced labor. Matthew Henry: "Their masters, who had abused them in their work, would have sent them away empty; but God provided that the labourers should not lose their hire." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **Fulfillment of prophecy.** This fulfills Genesis 15:14, where God promised Abraham his descendants would come out "with great possessions." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary

---

## v. 3: "The LORD gave the people favor… Moses himself was highly regarded."

- **Divine grace at work.** Precept Austin notes the Septuagint translates "favor" as *charis* (Greek for grace). God gave unmerited favor to the Israelites despite their own drift into Egyptian idolatry (Joshua 24:14). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **Moses' stature transformed.** Ellicott observes that "the man Moses" is a uniquely simple designation—others call him "prophet," "man of God," or "servant of the LORD," but never merely "the man." Whedon notes the Egyptians had become so panic-stricken that "Moses, Jehovah's dread messenger, overwhelmed them with awe and terror." This refers not to moral greatness but to the impression his role as God's instrument had produced. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html
- **Irony of Exodus 5:22.** Precept Austin contrasts this with the earlier accusation of the Hebrew foremen that Moses had "made us odious in Pharaoh's sight." Now, by the plagues, it was the *Egyptians* who held Moses in awe. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary

---

## v. 4: "About midnight I will go throughout Egypt."

- **God Himself carries out this plague.** Unlike previous plagues mediated through Moses and Aaron, here the LORD says "**I** am going out." Currid (cited at Precept Austin) notes the verb "go out" is the same used for Israel's exodus: "Because Pharaoh will not let God's people go out of Egypt, God will go out in Egypt!" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **Midnight terror.** Currid explains that nighttime was especially fearful for Egyptians because in the Hymn to the Aten, the sun-god's departure to the underworld meant the removal of divine protection. For Israel, by contrast, "He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Ps. 121:4). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **Timing of the Passover.** Whedon connects this: the lamb was selected on the 10th of Nisan (perhaps when the plague of darkness began) and killed on the 14th. During the three days of darkness the Israelites had light in their dwellings and waited for the final stroke, which fell on the night of the 14th, setting them free on the 15th. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html

---

## v. 5: "Every firstborn son… from the firstborn of Pharaoh… to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill… firstborn of all the cattle."

- **From highest to lowest.** The firstborn of Pharaoh (the "hereditary crown prince," *erpa suten sa*) to the lowest slave-girl represents the full social spectrum. Ellicott: "In every family there was to be one dead." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html
- **"Behind the hand mill."** Cole (cited by Guzik): "To sit 'behind the two mill stones' is to do the work of the lowest woman slave in the household, grinding corn (Isaiah 47:2)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/
- **The firstborn as the flower of the nation.** Whedon: "Israel consecrated all its firstborn to God, and Egypt's firstborn were taken in wrath, as were Israel's in mercy. The firstborn is the flower, the glory, of the nation." Under the law of primogeniture, this was "the most terrible blow that could be inflicted" (Thomas, cited by Guzik). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/
- **Cattle included: attack on Egyptian animal-worship.** Precept Austin explains that Egyptians attributed divine characteristics to many animals. Ellicott adds the remarkable note that four animals in Egypt were regarded as actual incarnations of deity—three bulls and one cow—and all were likely required to be firstborns, so their deaths would plunge Egypt into religious mourning as well as domestic grief. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html

---

## v. 6: "A great cry… such as has never been heard before and will never be heard again."

- **Unprecedented national grief.** Whedon calls this "awfully typical of that midnight cry which shall sound through all the earth: 'Behold, the Bridegroom cometh!'" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html
- **Poetic justice (talionic judgment).** Precept Austin notes the element of just retribution: "They had made Israel cry," and now God makes Egypt cry. Trapp (cited by Guzik) says: "They had made Israel cry: and God usually retaliates spoil to spoil (Ezekiel 39:10), number to number (Isaiah 65:11,12), choice to choice (Isaiah 66:3,4), cry to cry (James 5:1,4)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary

---

## v. 7: "Among all the Israelites, not even a dog will snarl."

- **Proverbial expression of perfect tranquility.** Ellicott calls it "evidently proverbial" (compare Joshua 10:21). Kaiser (cited by Guzik): "Among the Israelites there would be such tranquility on that evening that not a dog would have occasion to bark." The point is that the Egyptians would see clearly: the calamity was not Moses' or Israel's fault, but entirely Pharaoh's. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/
- **Whedon's reading:** "The very dogs of Egypt shall respect the people before whom their masters cower in fear." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html
- **Spurgeon (cited by Guzik):** "The Lord hath put a difference between those who are his people and those who are not. There are many distinctions among men which will one day be blotted out; but permit me to remind you at the outset that this is an eternal distinction." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/

---

## v. 8: "All these officials of yours will come and bow before me… And hot with anger, Moses left Pharaoh's presence."

- **Total reversal.** Guzik: "Moses' final words to Pharaoh told him that he and the rest of the Egyptians would command the people of Israel to go." Pharaoh's courtiers—not just commoners—would bow before Moses and beg Israel to leave. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/
- **Moses' anger.** Ellicott notes this is remarkable because Moses' speech itself was "calm and dignified," but he records what he felt: "For once his acquired 'meekness' failed, and the hot natural temper of his youth blazed up. His life had been threatened—he had been ignominiously dismissed… Under such circumstances, he 'did well to be angry.'" Whedon adds that this anger was "as Jehovah's messenger, representing his judicial wrath." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html
- **Moses shows restraint.** The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes that Moses "has the good feeling not to include the king himself in this abasement" when he says only Pharaoh's servants will bow. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/exodus/11.htm

---

## v. 9: "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied."

- **Summary statement.** This verse (with v.10) serves as a summary of all the previous nine plagues. Precept Austin: "This serves as summary statement of the 9 plagues." The purpose clause ("so that") introduces God's ultimate purpose: magnifying His power over all the false gods of Egypt. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-11-commentary
- **MacLaren** (Expositions) explains that Old Testament writers "are not wont to distinguish so sharply as more logical Westerns do between the actual result of an event and its purpose. With their deep faith in the all-ruling power of God, whatever had come to pass was what He had meant to come to pass." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/exodus-11.html
- **The nine plagues as a complete display.** Guzik: "The nine plagues can now be seen as a whole. They touched every phase of nature: mineral, animal, vegetable, human. They affected persons and property, and included all, from the highest to the lowest" (Thomas). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/

---

## v. 10: "The LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart."

This is the most theologically debated verse in the chapter. StudyLight's verse-by-verse page notes that "50 commentators divide six ways here—and 4 of them argue with each other," breaking down as: Calvinist 15, Arminian 7, Dispensational 11, Lutheran 2, Catholic 1, Stance not recorded 6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/11-10.html

### Traditional reading (shared across most traditions):

- **God hardened only after Pharaoh hardened himself.** This is the most common traditional interpretation. Guzik: "Here for the fourth time we are told that God hardened Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12, 10:20, 10:27, and 11:10). Yet God never hardened Pharaoh's heart until he first hardened it against the LORD and His people (Exodus 7:13, 7:22, 8:15, 8:19, 8:32, and 9:7)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/
- **Ellicott** states it as point 5 of his summary: "God had hardened his heart, as a judgment upon him, after he had first himself hardened it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html
- **Matthew Henry** (Reformed/Nonconformist): God's hardening is a judicial act on an already wicked man. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/11-10.html
- **MacLaren**: "God hardens no man's heart who has not first hardened it himself." He also offers the analogy: "The same fire softens wax and hardens clay. Whosoever is not brought near is driven farther off, by the influences which God brings to bear on us." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/exodus-11.html

### Reformed perspective:

- **D.A. Carson** (Monergism): Carson argues against the simple sequential pattern ("Pharaoh hardened → God hardened"). He contends that "no simple pattern is discernible in these references" and that the three formulations (God hardened / Pharaoh's heart was hardened / Pharaoh hardened his heart) are "mutually complementary." He makes three observations: (a) Pharaoh was already a wicked man; God was pronouncing judgment, not hardening a morally neutral person. (b) In a theistic universe, divine hardening and human self-hardening are not disjunctive. (c) This pattern appears elsewhere in Scripture (1 Kings 22, Ezekiel 14:9, 2 Thessalonians 2:11-12). — https://www.monergism.com/blog/%E2%80%9Ci-will-harden-his-heart-so-he-will-not-let-people-go%E2%80%9D
- The Reformed view emphasizes divine sovereignty: God's hardening serves His purpose of multiplying wonders and displaying His glory. — https://www.monergism.com/content/why-did-god-harden-pharaoh%E2%80%99s-heart-case-divine-ultimacy

### Methodist / Arminian perspective:

- **Whedon's Commentary** (Methodist): Whedon emphasizes that the plagues were "intended, as they were, to soften" but became "a cause of hardening." The cumulative refusal brought judicial hardening. Whedon's overall framework stresses human responsibility and the progressive nature of judgment—"judgments unheeded inevitably lead on to sorer judgments, till destruction comes." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-11.html

### Summary of traditional interpretive angles on "hardening":

All traditions represented in the searched sites agree on several points: (1) Pharaoh was not a neutral or innocent party—he was already an oppressor; (2) divine hardening is a judicial act on a heart already self-hardened; (3) the same wonders that should have produced repentance instead produced greater obstinacy, and God sovereignly used this for His purposes. Where they differ is emphasis: Reformed sources stress divine sovereignty and decree; Arminian/Methodist sources stress progressive human choice and the natural consequences of rejecting light.

---

## Additional Tradition-Specific Notes

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):
- Guzik emphasizes the complete reversal of power: those in power would be forced to obey. The plundering is God's provision and justice. The theme is that "God tells His children that while the enemy may seem powerful… in the final act, when the curtain rises, Jesus wins and since we are in Christ, we win." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/

### Anglican (Ellicott):
- Ellicott pays careful attention to the Hebrew text and historical Egyptian context, such as the title of the crown prince (*erpa suten sa*) and the religious significance of firstborn sacred animals. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-11.html

### Baptist / Spurgeon:
- Spurgeon's comment on v.7 (preserved in Guzik) about the "eternal distinction" between God's people and the world reflects a classic Baptist emphasis on the visible separation of the redeemed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-11/

---

*Sources searched: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, studylight.org (Gill, Ellicott, Whedon, MacLaren, Matthew Henry), biblehub.com (Expositor's, Clarke, Poole), monergism.com. Catholic/Orthodox and modern scholarship sources could not be reached within search limits; those traditions are therefore not represented in these notes.*
